title: Jehoiada Crowns Joash and Restores the Covenant
summary: In the seventh year of Athaliah's rule, the priest Jehoiada organizes a covenant with army commanders, Levites, and family heads, and brings the hidden seven-year-old Joash into the temple, where he is crowned, given the Testimony, and anointed king. Athaliah rushes in crying treason and is taken out of the temple and executed. Jehoiada leads the king and people in a covenant to be the LORD's people, the temple of Baal is destroyed, temple worship is restored in order, and Joash is seated on the throne while the city is at peace.
story: Chapter 22 ended with David's line reduced to one hidden child and Athaliah, Ahab's daughter, ruling Judah. This chapter tells how the lamp of David was set back on its stand. The priest Jehoiada acts as the guardian of both the Davidic promise and the temple, and the coup is carried out largely by priests and Levites inside the house of God. The chapter moves from secrecy to public celebration, from usurpation to covenant, and from the worship of Baal to the restored worship of the LORD. Chapter 24 will show Joash's reign flourishing while Jehoiada lives and falling apart after he dies.
historical:
Athaliah ruled about six years, around 841 to 835 BC, and Joash then reigned forty years (24:1), about 835 to 796 BC. The parallel account in 2 Kings 11 tells the same story but with some different emphases. In Kings the guards who protect the young king include the Carites (probably foreign mercenaries) and the royal guard; in Chronicles the Levites, the commanders of hundreds, and the heads of families play the leading role, and the text insists that only consecrated priests and Levites entered the temple building. Many scholars think the Chronicler has shaped the account to show the coup carried out in accordance with the law's rules for the sanctuary; others think he draws on additional information about the Levites' role. Both accounts agree on the core events.

The temple of Baal in Jerusalem was presumably established under Athaliah's influence, continuing the Baal worship that her mother Jezebel had promoted in the north. Jehu had already destroyed Baal's temple in Samaria (2 Kings 10:18-28). Mattan, the priest of Baal, is otherwise unknown.
cultural:
Temple service was organized in divisions of priests and Levites that rotated on and off duty, changing over on the Sabbath (1 Chronicles 24). Jehoiada's plan used the changeover, keeping both the incoming and outgoing divisions on duty so that he had twice the usual number of men in the temple without arousing suspicion. The spears and shields of King David stored in the temple were weapons dedicated there, and using them to protect David's heir had symbolic force.

The coronation included several elements. The crown marked royal office. The Testimony was probably a written document of the covenant law or royal obligations; Deuteronomy 17:18-20 required the king to have a copy of the law and read it all his life, and many interpreters connect the Testimony with that command. Anointing with oil set the king apart for God's service, and the shout "Long live the king" was the people's acclamation. Tearing one's clothes, as Athaliah did, was a traditional sign of grief or alarm. The king's pillar at the temple entrance seems to have been a customary place where a king stood on public occasions.
literary: The chapter has three movements: preparation (verses 1 to 10), revolution (verses 11 to 15), and restoration (verses 16 to 21). The word covenant occurs three times and structures the story: a covenant with the commanders (verse 1), a covenant of the assembly with the king (verse 3), and a covenant that king and people would be the LORD's (verse 16). Jehoiada's speech in verse 3 grounds the whole action in the promise concerning the descendants of David. The scene of the coronation is vivid with sound: people running and cheering, trumpets, singers, and Athaliah's scream of "Treason, treason" set against the people's shout of long live the king. The last verse brings the story to rest, echoing the peace and rest given to faithful kings earlier in the book: the people rejoiced and the city was quiet.

outline.t: Jehoiada makes a covenant and presents the king's son
The plan: priests, Levites, and guards in position
Joash crowned, given the Testimony, and anointed
Athaliah cries treason and is executed
Covenant renewal, Baal's temple destroyed, worship restored, and the king enthroned

doctrines.note: Jehoiada leads king and people into a covenant that they would be the LORD's people. The restoration of David's line is joined to the renewal of the relationship between God and his people.
Jehoiada declares that the king's son must reign as the LORD promised concerning David's descendants. The anointing of Joash is an act of faith in that promise at the moment it seemed lost.

The plan takes care that only consecrated priests and Levites enter the temple, that Athaliah is not killed in the house of the LORD, and that gatekeepers keep out anything unclean. Even in a revolution, the holiness of God's house is respected.

words.note: Berit, covenant. A binding agreement with obligations, often sworn before God. It appears three times in this chapter, and the final covenant, that king and people would be the LORD's, recalls the basic covenant formula of the Old Testament: I will be your God, and you will be my people.

Edut, testimony, a word often used for the covenant law, as in the tablets of the Testimony kept in the ark. Given to Joash at his coronation, it probably represents the written law or covenant obligations under which he was to rule.
Mashach, to anoint. Pouring oil on the king set him apart for his office. From this verb comes mashiach, anointed one, which becomes the title Messiah and, through Greek, Christ.
Qesher, conspiracy or treason. Athaliah's cry uses it against the very people restoring the lawful line. The irony is sharp: the usurper accuses the rightful king's supporters of treason.

christ: Joash is an anointed son of David brought out from hiding and proclaimed king against a usurper, and the chapter's central claim is that he must reign because of God's promise concerning David's descendants. The New Testament proclaims Jesus as the Anointed One (the meaning of Christ) and the Son of David who reigns by that same promise (Acts 2:30-36). Jehoiada's covenant, that king and people would be the LORD's, looks forward to the new covenant in which God's people belong to him through Christ (Hebrews 8:8-10). Joash himself later failed badly (chapter 24), which is part of why the Old Testament's hope pointed beyond any one king of Judah. The link is the Davidic promise, not an allegory of the details.

hard.q: Was it right for a priest to lead an armed coup, and to have Athaliah and the priest of Baal killed?
hard.a: The chapter presents Jehoiada's action as the restoration of the lawful king, not as a rebellion. Athaliah had seized the throne by murdering the royal heirs, and in the Chronicler's view she had no right to it; Joash was the legitimate heir by God's promise to David. Her execution and Mattan's death are reported as judgments on murder and on the promotion of Baal worship, which Israel's law treated as capital crimes (Deuteronomy 13). Many readers still feel the weight of the violence. Christian interpreters have generally treated the chapter as a record of God preserving his promise in Israel's history rather than as a model for how the church should act. The New Testament gives the church no sword and calls it to suffer rather than to seize power (Romans 12:17-21). Others have drawn on this chapter in debates about whether it is ever right to resist a tyrant, a question on which Christian traditions have disagreed.

questions: Jehoiada waited six years before acting. What does his patience teach about the timing of faithful action?
The covenant in verse 16 was that the king and the people would be the LORD's people. What would it mean for your household or community to make that commitment together?
The chapter ends with rejoicing and a quiet city. What would have to be removed from your life for real peace to come?
